nodes.body: It is the end-of-season sale at the old Heddle Lock boatyard. Three tables of other people's things stand out in the drizzle. Canvas covers sag overhead. In a shoebox full of odd bits there is a worn enamel compass. It sits among rusty shackles, windlass handles, and a single brass porthole rim. The compass face is the colour of canal water. Six small marks and a wavy line are scratched into its case. They show through the scuffs when it is tilted just so against the weak light.

choices.label: Open the case and read the card.

nodes.body: Folded into eighths inside the leather case is a card. It is soft as a dock leaf. Spidery ink on it reads: THE REACHES. Under that are six lock names on the old Wendover Arm, a cut that only half exists any more. The last entry is PUMPHOUSE. A row of six figures is written below. Four of them are crossed out with the same nib. Mr Okonjo, who is running the sale, says the box came out of a narrowboat called the *Kingfisher*. It was put away last March. Her owner ran the canal group for thirty years.

choices.label: Ask Mr Okonjo about the boat.
Start at the nearest mark on the casing.
Take the card to the waterways archives.

nodes.body: Mr Okonjo has cleared eleven boats this year. He remembers every one of them. The papers for the *Kingfisher* sit in a blue folder in the back of his van. The owner was a man called Harold Locke. He died in February. One of his boxes has not been priced yet. It is a wooden tool chest, still locked. It felt heavy when they carried it off the boat.

choices.label: Ask to see the unpriced box.

nodes.body: Hold it up to the pearly sky. The wavy line is the canal. The six marks sit along it. Their order is not the order on the card. The nearest of them is fifteen minutes away at the old guillotine lock. That is a dry spillway now. A picnic bench stands where the gates used to be.

Priya is behind the desk. She has been waiting most of a year for someone to walk in and ask a question with a boat name in it.

The six marks turn out to be six real places. The walk from one to the next takes two hours in the rain. It answers nothing at all. We find four bare lock posts, a picnic bench, and a padlock. It is a very good map of a waterway that has changed. The card goes back into the case.

The door under the pump house is steel in a brick arch and the padlock is a four-wheel combination gone green. It turns freely on the first two wheels and stiffly on the last two, which is a fact worth more than any guess.

Behind the door is a winch with a frayed cable. There are four lock gate paddles and a stack of survey maps. One edge of the maps has rotted into grey mush. A typed card is taped to the inside of the door. It says the society will come back. It is less than the cut remembers, and more than the clipboard was told.

The flatbed is early, the men are quick and the store is empty by twenty past eight. The skip goes out of the yard at nine with a Tirfor winch in it that nobody photographed. The padlock, still locked, is left hanging on the open hasp.

nodes.body: The third order is the one the Trust news printed in 1987. It opens the lock at twenty past seven on Thursday evening. Two mooring holders, a notebook, and a woman of eighty-six are there. They stand on the cobbles behind, and for a moment no one says a word.

Joan Arkwright spends an hour with a grease gun and a wire brush. On a Thursday evening, she shows how the winch works on the pump house steps in front of six people. Three butty boat hatches open across the basin and stay open until she is done.

The marina boss signs for a Tirfor winch, four paddles, a tripod, and two tool chests on Friday morning. That was the day the flatbed truck had been booked. The flatbed takes only the real junk. A fix-up work party comes the next summer, and it is not very smooth yet.

The store is cleared right on time, with a list made first. So, four cases, a minute book, and a box of photos come out before the skip bin does. After that, all the rest goes. It is not the week anyone wanted. And it is not the week that would have been if the phone call had been made on Tuesday.

The four shapes make a date. It is written the way a club helper might say it: the first Saturday in December 1961. Once you spot it, you can't not see it. You figure it out at ten past nine on Friday morning. That is one hour and ten minutes after the flat lorry left.

No one in charge is in the yard on Friday morning. The folder sits in a bag on a boat table across the water. The store is empty by twenty past eight. The lock was the whole worry, but it was never the real problem.

Eleven tools. A room. One evening a week. And one grown-up who will say yes. Every one of those is here along the Wendover Arm, except the last one. And that is the one someone has to ask for out loud.

The name on the tool box is the granddad from the next boat spot. He helped fix the canal until he was twenty-two. He has not said so out loud in fifty years. He takes the box back. Then, two weeks later, he brings it to a work day.

nodes.body: Two copies, one signature each, a list of eleven items and a date. It is done on a Tuesday evening in the marina workshop. The mooring holders watch. It is the least exciting twenty minutes of the whole two weeks. And it is the only reason nothing falls apart later.

There is a minute book from 1934. There are four hundred photos. There is a run of rally programmes and one card headed THE REACHES. Each item is numbered, put on a shelf, and stamped on the back. Priya puts the compass photo in the display case by the door.

Ellie leaves the plaque uncovered and moves the chalkboard a foot to the left. For about a month people come into the narrowboat café to look at a piece of enamel and buy tea while they are there. Then they stop, and the plaque stays.

ending.title: The Plaque Under the Menu Board

nodes.body: The story runs on Friday. It sits under a photo of an empty store and a skip. It is a good piece of writing about something that has already happened. Four people write in. They say they would have helped if anybody had asked them on Tuesday.

There are eleven people, one borrowed winch, a photocopied map, and six enamel plaques. The work party stops at all six reaches in the cold. It clears scrub badly at each one. More people follow it round than anybody expected. Half of them are under twelve.

Forty people walk the route on a Saturday in October. They walk behind a woman of eighty-six. She stops at each plaque and says what was cleared there. At the guillotine lock there is no plaque at all. Everybody stands on the concrete spillway and listens anyway.

Five plaques go back onto five piers with the right brass screws. The sixth is cut new in enamel by a sign-writer on the industrial estate. He will not take money for it. It goes onto the guillotine lock pier. It fits the rectangle that has been waiting thirty years.

ending.title: Six Plaques Back on Six Piers

nodes.body: The compass goes back into the leather case. The card is folded into eighths beside it. It lives on a shelf. It is taken out and traced with a thumb about once a week. It is the only object in the story that ends up exactly where it started. And it means something completely different.

ending.title: The Compass Goes Back in Its Case

nodes.body: Tools go to the workshop. Paper goes to the archives. The photograph goes to the butty boats. Plaques go to the piers. The card goes to the collection with a note saying who found it. It takes three weeks of small dull errands. Nothing is left in a bag under anybody's bunk.

The store comes out onto the cobbles. It gets listed, photographed, and divided into keep and skip. This is done in front of two men who are being paid by the hour. They are surprisingly interested. The room under the pump house ends the week swept, dry, and empty.

The skip leaves the yard at nine on Friday morning. It has a Tirfor winch and four wooden cases in it. There is a photo of it going. It is taken from the basin gate. The newsletter will not print the photo because there is nothing to say about it.

Three separate adults would have stopped it. None of them were told. Asking felt like a bigger thing on Wednesday. It turned out to be a small thing on the following Monday when all three said so in turn.

The last order is wrong. The wheels go back to zero. The trail ran from a shoebox in a boatyard through six piers and sixty years. It ends at a steel door in a cold basin. A flatbed is booked for the morning.

ending.title: The Trail Ends at a Steel Door
